newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major rules out pre-election shift over EMU.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major rules out pre-election shift over EMU.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major risked reopening splits in his Conservative party on Tuesday, firmly ruling out a change before the next election in Britain's wait-and-see stance on the European Union's single currency.

Major has been under pressure from "Euro-sceptic" Conservatives opposed to closer European ties to declare before the election, due by May, that Britain would not be in the first group of states switching to the currency when it is launched in 1999.
But Major, whose six years as prime minister have been dogged by party splits over Europe, said in parliament he would not change his policy before polling day.

Asked by opposition Labour party leader Tony Blair for an assurance that the government's policy had not changed, Major surprised members of parliament by stating simply: "This remains unequivocally the position of the government".

Blair had been hoping to make political capital out of recent reports that Major was considering a pre-election declaration that Britain's chances of signing up for economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999 was very remote.

Speculation has been rife that Clarke would resign if Major, who secured an opt-out from EMU when it was negotiated at Maastricht in 1991, bowed to the Euro-sceptics and hardened his stance against the single currency.
"It's right to give you credit for such a clear reply," Blair, caught off guard, answered. Labour's EMU position mirrors that of the Conservatives after a change of policy last month.
In a second attempt to make Major squirm, Blair then asked Major whether he agreed with Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine that the position would remain unchanged this side of the election.
"Mr Heseltine said that. That is our position," the prime minister confirmed.

Major's forthright comments were immediately interpreted by political commentators as a victory for Clarke and Heseltine, the cabinet's two leading pro-Europeans, who have been fighting a rearguard action for the past year against the Euro-sceptics.

The disappointment the Euro-sceptics felt at Major's remarks was tempered by a statement from Clarke that he had secured confirmation from fellow EU finance ministers that Britain would not be bound by regulations governing the single currency.
A new bout of infighting over Europe is the last thing Major needs given the Conservatives' deep unpopularity.
A poll in the Guardian newspaper on Tuesday suggested last week's budget had only made matters worse, despite a one penny cut in the standard rate of income tax.
The poll by the ICM group showed Labour had widened its lead to 19 percentage points from 13.

"We have to be cautious about drawing conclusions from a single poll," said one elections expert. "But if this trend is confirmed, it is hard to see how the Tories (Conservatives) can hope to stay in power."
